INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
The Roderick and Solange MacArthur Justice
Center (“RSMJC”) is a civil rights non-profit
organization founded in 1985 by the family of
J. Roderick MacArthur to advocate for human rights
and social justice through litigation. Through its
Supreme Court and Appellate Program, RSMJC

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no counsel for a party (nor a party itself) made a monetary
contribution intended to fund the preparation or submission of
this brief. No person other than amici or their counsel made a
monetary contribution to this brief’s preparation or submission.

2

litigates cases before this Court and appellate courts
nationwide in order to vindicate the civil rights of
persons who have been subjected to mistreatment by
the criminal legal system. In particular, RSMJC
regularly represents incarcerated people in federal
prisons who have attempted to use the Bureau of
Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program to seek
administrative relief. This experience gives RSMJC
expertise in and perspective into the ways in which
the grievance procedure fails to address serious
medical issues like those at issue in this case.
The Prison Policy Initiative (“PPI”) is a non-profit,
non-partisan research organization that studies the
broader harm of mass criminalization and advocates
for concrete reforms to bring about a more just society.
PPI specializes in analyses of national and state level
data relating to the criminal justice system and
transforms these data into powerful and informative
graphics. PPI conducted an extensive review of data
from the Administrative Remedy Program in a study
revealing the procedure’s systematic failure to provide
meaningful relief.

3

INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Francis Nielsen asks this Court to
narrow or eliminate Carlson v. Green , 446 U.S. 14
(1980), and the crucial protections it provides based
on a clear historical error. In Petitioner’s mind, the
Bureau of Prisons created the Administrative Remedy
Program in 1979, years after the events at issue in
Carlson. Br. for Petitioner at 10. Based on that
assumption, Petitioner claims that the Carlson Court
never considered this grievance procedure, and that
alone makes any subsequent case—even one factually
identical to Carlson—a new Bivens context. See id.
at 32. Petitioner is simply wrong about history.
Norman A. Carlson—the Director of the Bureau of
Prisons and named defendant in Carlson—instituted
the Administrative Remedy Program in 1974, more
than a year before the even ts at issue in that case.
Drawing on input from Chief Justice Warren Burger
and other federal judges, Carlson envisioned the
procedure as an added way for incarcerated people
and prison officials to resolve issues, especially minor
ones that did not require judicial review. In 1973,
Carlson conducted a pilot program in three federal
prisons, before implementing the Administrative
Remedy Program across the Bureau of Prisons’
facilities the following year. When Carlson notified
Congress of the full implemen tation, he was explicit
that this procedure would not supplant the federal
courts, emphasizing that an incarcerated person
“may, if he chooses, . . . file his law suit directly with
the appropriate court.” 120 Cong. Rec. 8300 (Mar. 26,
1974).
Accordingly, the Administrative Remedy Program
was in effect when Joseph Jones, Jr., died in custody

4

at the federal penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana.
The plaintiff’s complaint in Carlson even noted that
letters were sent to Carlson challenging the prison’s
notoriously inadequate medical care. The Supreme
Court not only had this information when it decided
the case, but also knew about the Administrative
Remedy Program from Chief Justice Burger’s
involvement in its creation. Accordingly, the basic
premise of Petitioner’s argument is incorrect. That is
reason enough to reject it.
Petitioner’s argument is deeply flawed for another
reason, as well. Petitioner portrays the
Administrative Remedy Program as an alternative
remedial scheme, but it is anything but that. As more
than a decade of data shows, claims raising serious
medical issues like those suffered by Respondent
Kekai Watanabe are almost always rejected in the
Administrative Remedy Program. Specifically,
amicus Prison Policy Initiative’s study found that
relief was granted in less than 1% of cases. This
abysmal rate reflects the many traps in the system
that ensnare meritorious claims, including the rigid
application of byzantine rules and deadlines, prison
officials’ inaction and delays, and outright misconduct
like obstruction and retaliation.
As a result, Bivens actions are critical for ensuring
that adequate medical care is provided to people in
federal prisons. Petitioner’s notion that federal courts
should abdicate their responsibility for preserving the
Eighth Amendment’s guarantee of adequate medical
care because the Administrative Remedy Program, of
all things, is filling that role is farcical.

5

ARGUMENT
I. The Bureau Of Prisons Instituted The
Administrative Remedy Program In 1974,
Before The Events At Issue In Carlson.
The Bureau of Prisons (“BOP”) instituted its
modern administrative grievance procedure six years
before Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980), and more
than a year before the events at issue in that case. See
Green v. Carlson , 581 F.2d 669, 670 (7th Cir. 1978)
(noting Joseph Jones, Jr.’s death in August 1975).
Effective April 1, 1974, th e Director of the BOP,
Norman A. Carlson, instituted the “Administrative
Remedy Procedure” (“ARP”) to “handle complaints
from inmates in Federal correctional institutions.”
120 Cong. Rec. 8300 (Mar. 26, 1974); see J. MICHAEL
KEATING, JR. ET AL ., GRIEVANCE MECHANISMS IN
CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTIONS 36 (1975) (noting that
“[a]ll persons in the care of the Bureau, or
approximately 23,000 prisoners, are served by the
procedure”).2 “The system has remained intact and
substantively unchanged since that time.” David M.
Bierie, Procedural Justice a nd Prison Violence:
Examining Complaints Among Federal Inmates
(2000—2007), 19 Psychol. Pub. Pol’y & L. 15, 16
(2013).
Like the ARP in effect today, the ARP adopted in
1974 provided an opportunity for informal resolution,
followed by “three levels of review” initiated by the
filing of a formal grievance. Bruce Bernstein, The
Federal Bureau of Prisons Administrative Grievance
Procedure: An Effective Alternative to Prisoner

2 https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000213973.

6

Litigation, 13 AM. CRIM. L. REV. 779, 779 (1976). The
procedure encouraged prison officials “to resolve
problems via informal acti on before the filing of a
formal grievance.” Id at 784. If those efforts were
unsuccessful, the incarcerated person could “trigger
the operation of the mechanism by filing an official
complaint with the warden’s office.” Id. at 785. From
there, the person could appeal to the Regional
Director “overseeing the prisons in his region,” and
then to “the General Counsel’s Office of the Bureau in
Washington, D.C.” Id. In October 1974, the BOP
ordered 50,000 copies of the forms used to initiate the
three levels of review—B P-DIR-9, BP-DIR-10, and
BP-DIR-11—for distribution to its prisons, including
2,200 forms for the federal penitentiary at Terre
Haute, Indiana, where the events of Carlson took
place. See App. 23-24 (Operations Memorandum
2001.15, Fed. Bureau of Prisons (Oct. 10, 1974)).
In adopting the ARP, Carlson made clear that “the
new procedure [was] not intended to supplant legal
avenues of redress for prisoner grievances.” 120 Cong.
Rec. 8300. Rather, the ARP was designed to provide
“an additional vehicle for internal solution of
problems.” Id. Carlson emphasized that an
incarcerated person “may, if he chooses, . . . file his
law suit directly with the appropriate court.” Id.
Carlson did so knowing that there had “been an
increase in the number of suits filed by inmates
naming specific staff members as defendants.”
App. 21 (Operations Me morandum 2001.14, Fed.
Bureau of Prisons (Sept. 27, 1974)).
Keeping access to federal courts open was
consistent with the BOP’s prior practice. Before the
ARP, the primary means for raising issues in federal

7

prisons was the prison mailbox. See Administrative
Ombudsman: Hearing on S. 1195 Before the
Subcomm. on Admin. Prac. and Proc. of the S. Comm.
on the Judiciary , 90th Cong. 35 (Jan. 16, 1968)
(statement of Dr. Myrl E.  Alexander, Dir. of the
Bureau of Prisons).3 Each federal prison maintained a
“special letterbox” through which letters could be
“forwarded unopened” to “the Attorney General; to
any Congressman or Senator; to the Board of Parole;
to any Federal judge; to the Director, Bureau of
Prisons; and others in Government.” Id. Under that
system, “access to the courts” was “open and
unrestricted.” Id. at 37. The BOP’s rules made clear
that any letters addressed to federal courts would “be
separated from other [prison mailbox] correspondence
and forwarded directly to the addressee without
inspection,” and “at government expense.”
Corrections: Hearing before Subcomm. No. 3 of the H.
Comm. on the Judiciary, Part III – Prisoners’
Representation, 92nd Cong. 130 (Nov. 10, 1971)
(reproduction of BOP Policy Statement 7300.2A—
Prisoners Mail Box (Dec. 28, 1967)). Reflecting on the
prison mailbox system, Carlson’s predecessor, Myrl
Alexander, noted that denying federal prisoners the
ability to raise issues directly with courts and other
outside institutions “would  be stupid indeed,” and
that communication through the prison mailbox was

3 The BOP also maintained a “chaotic and ineffective” procedure
known as the “Cop-Out,” by which an incarcerated person
“informally lodge[d] his complaint with the prison
administration, but no specific official within the institution
[was] appointed to receive such complaints.” Bernstein, supra,
at 783. There was no requirement that any response be provided,
or any other “system-wide rules” governing the procedure. Id.
The “inadequacies” of this procedure were “obvious.” Id. at 784.

8

“the most valuable safety valve of the entire system.”
Administrative Ombudsman Hearing , supra, at 35-
36.
Rather than supplant federal courts, a primary
purpose of the ARP was to address more efficiently
minor disputes for which judicial review was
unnecessary. In announcing the ARP in 1974, Carlson
cited Chief Justice Warren Burger as a key
inspiration for the procedure. 120 Cong. Rec. 8300
(Mar. 26, 1974); see also Federal Bureau of Prisons,
Annual Report – 1973 , at 24 (noting that “Chief
Justice Warren E. Burger suggested” developing the
procedure).4 In a report on the federal judiciary in
1973, Chief Justice Burger asked whether “other and
better methods may be available” to address the
growing number of petitions concerning disputes like
a prison official taking “seven packages of cigarettes”
away from an incarcerated person, without “making a
federal case out of it.” Warren E. Burger, Report on the
Federal Judicial Branch—1973 , 59 A.B.A.J. 1125,
1128 (1973). Chief Justice Burger made clear he was
not suggesting “at all that federal courts deny
protection”; rather, he pr oposed “that we use some
common sense and devise procedures that give
prompt attention to valid complaints without calling
on eleven federal judges and a train of other public
employees to deal with three dollars worth of
cigarettes.” Id. For such matters, Chief Justice Burger
thought it would be “sheer nonsense” to “engage the
primary attention of one district judge twice, three
circuit judges on appeal, and six others in a secondary
sense—to say nothings of lawyers, court clerks,

4 https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=coo.31924112763275.

9

bailiffs, court reporters, and all the rest.” Id.5
Consistent with Chief Justice Burger’s input, Carlson
also cited a meeting with judges of the Eighth Circuit
Court of Appeals, who told him that their “dockets
were overwhelmed with inmate complaints” about
“such trivial matters as ill-fitting shoes and breakfast
cereal that was cold.” John W. Roberts, View from the
Top, 1 Fed. Prisons J. 27, 40 (1990) (excerpting
Nov. 30, 1989 interview with Carlson); see also
App. 18 (Letter from Hon. Adrian A. Spears, District
Judge, W.D. Texas, to Norman Carlson, Dir. Federal
Bureau of Prisons (Mar. 14, 1974)) (noting the
proposed ARP allowed some grievances to “be handled
administratively,” “especially those that do not rise to
the constitutional level”).
Although the ARP had been in effect since 1974,
the BOP did not formally seek to publish the rules
governing the procedure until 1977. See 42 Fed. Reg.
64082 (Dec. 21, 1977). The BOP did so in response to
a final judgment issued by the United States District
Court for the District of Columbia on February 16,
1977. See App. 9 (Civil Docket Sheet, Ramer v.
Kleindienst, Civil Action No. 294-73 (D.D.C.)). In that
case, two federal prisoners sued the U.S. Attorney
General and Carlson under the Administrative
Procedure Act, challenging the BOP’s failure to

5 See also Sparks v. Fuller , 506 F.2d 1238, 1239 (1st Cir. 1974)
(urging prisons to resolve minor issues like whether incarcerated
people could keep cats as pets); C LEMENS BARTOLLAS, A MODEL
OF CORRECTIONAL LEADERSHIP: THE CAREER OF NORMAN A.
CARLSON 141 (2010) (“Norm wanted to come up with a procedure
to expedite the courts’ handling of what seemed to be impossible
caseloads from federal correctional institutions, often of a trivial
or minor nature.”).

10

publish its policy statements in the Federal Register.
See App. 15 (Complaint at ¶ 12, Ramer, Civil Action
No. 294-73 (Feb. 15, 1973)). The plaintiffs argued that
the BOP’s failure to publish deprived them of
“adequate notice or knowledge of the rules and
requirements embodied in the ‘policy statements.’”
App. 15-16 ( Id. ¶ 13). In 1977, the district court
directed the defendants to publish “certain rules and
regulations” addressed in the suit. See App. 9 (Civil
Docket Sheet, Ramer, Civil Action No. 294-73).
To comply with that judgment, the BOP published
the ARP. See 44 Fed. Reg. 62248 (O ct. 29, 1979) (“A
consent order entered in the U.S. District Court for
the District of Columbia pertaining to aspects of the
Administrative Remedy Procedure requires an
implementation date of November 1, 1979.”). Carlson
ordered all BOP wardens to “post copies of these
regulations in the places that will ensure the widest
coverage,” including the “law library.” App. 67
(Operations Memorandum 2200.1 CH-2, Bureau of
Prisons (Dec. 29, 1977)). The proposed rules noted
that the BOP’s processes were previously set forth in
“Policy Statements and Operations Memoranda.”
42 Fed. Reg. 64082 (Dec. 21, 1977). Following the
notice and comment period, the BOP published the
final rules in 1979. 44 Fed. Reg. 62248 (Oct. 29, 1979).
As the above history shows, the ARP was in effect
during the events at issue in Carlson. On August 15,
1975, Joseph Jones, Jr. died while in federal custody
at Terre Haute, due to an asthma attack brought on
by prison officials’ failure to treat his known condition.
Green, 581 F.2d at 671. At the time, the ARP had been
available to raise medical is sues for over a year; in
fact, Carlson specifically directed prison wardens to

11

track grievances raising “Medical” issues. See App. 19-
20 (Operational Memorandum 2001.11, Fed. Bureau
of Prisons (Apr. 29, 1974)); see also  App. 25-26, 29
(Norman A. Carlson, Director’s Letter (Dec. 19, 1974))
(attaching chart showing that 14 medical grievances
were filed at Terre Haute from April to September
1974); App. 30, 35 (Norman A. Carlson, Director’s
Letter (Apr. 8, 1976)) (attach ing chart showing that
32 medical grievances were filed at Terre Haute in
1975). Mr. Jones’s mother’s complaint indicated that
“[l]etters were written to Director CARLSON and
Warden BENSON complaining of the lack of proper
medical care” at Terre Haute, which had led to the
deaths of multiple incarcerated people. App. at 11,
Carlson, 446 U.S. 14 (No. 78-1261), 1979 U.S. S. Ct.
Briefs LEXIS 1541, at *14; see also id. at *26
(defendants admitting “complaint letters were
received about the medical facilities”). Mr. Jones could
have used the ARP to challenge the inadequate care
he received, although he would not have been
obligated to do so, as it expressly provided that he
could “file his law suit dire ctly with the appropriate
court.” Civil Rights for Institutionalized Persons:
Hearings on H.R. 2439 and H.R. 5791 Before the
Subcomm. on Courts, Civil Liberties & the Admin. of
Justice of the H. Comm. on the Judiciary , 95th Cong.
714 (1977) (reproduction of Bureau of Prisons Policy
Statement 2001.6A (Oct. 18, 1974)).
Therefore, Petitioner is incorrect when he claims
that the ARP “became effective in late 1979,” “years
after [Mr. Jones’s] death in that case.” Br. for
Petitioner 32, 38. Mr. Jones “could have used” the
ARP in 1975, id. at 38, as the Supreme Court would
have known in Carlson—especially given Chief
Justice Burger’s role in the procedure’s creation.

12

Indeed, in his 1976 report on the condition of the
federal judiciary, Chief Justice Burger specifically
commented on “the past year’s experience” with the
ARP. Warren E. Burger, The Condition of the
Judiciary: Year-End Report (Jan. 3, 1976); see also
Federal Bureau of Prisons, Annual Report – 1976 ,
at 8.6
II. The ARP Has Become A System For
Rejecting Claims, Providing Relief For
Less Than 1% Of Medical Grievances.
Petitioner’s argument based on the ARP is deeply
flawed for another reason, as well. Petitioner suggests
that the ARP provides a remedy today that was
“unavailable in Carlson.” Br. for Petitioner 38. But the
truth is quite the opposite. Far from providing
remedies, the ARP is a buzzsaw for denying requests
for relief, especially those raising serious medical
issues.
Medical care in prisons, and specifically in the
Federal Bureau of Prisons, has long been notoriously
inadequate. See, e.g. , App. 48 (Robert L. Brutsche,
Summary of Terre Haute Medical Problems Over the
Past 1½ Years (Sept. 23, 1976)) (finding “significant
problems” in Mr. Jones’s care, including the “lack of
aggressive treatment in the face of acute asthmatic
symptoms” and “failure of the physician to come to the
hospital despite several ca lls”); App. 82 (George A.
Ralston, Jr., Advisory Report on U.S. Penitentiary
Terre Haute, at 15 (Jan. 6, 1982)) (concluding the
Terre Haute hospital “failed to provide adequate
procedures and safeguards for proper inmate care”);

6 https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=coo.31924112763275.

13

Walter Pavlo, Bureau of Prisons Continues To Have
Issues With Medical Care: OIG , F ORBES (Jan. 14,
2026).7 Multiple OIG investigations of individual
cases or facilities have revealed systemic problems
with medical care within the Bureau of Prisons,
caused by chronic staffing shortages, a lack of
appropriate follow-up care, and a lack of attention to
urgent medical issues. See, e.g., U.S. Department of
Justice, Office of the Inspector General, Investigation
and Review of the Federal Bureau of Prisons’
Conditions of Confinement and Medical Treatment of
Frederick Mervin Bardell and Related
Representations to the Court, Upon Referral by Senior

incarcerated people not only directly benefits
incarcerated people themselves, but also correctional
officers and other staff. While incarcerated people
experience medical neglect directly, prison staff are
impacted by the consequenc es, as well. For example,
61% of correctional supervisors witnessed an

conditions contribute to 34% of corrections officers

reporting depression. See Health, P RISON POLICY

to continue only exacerbates the burden for prison
staff and administrators.
The low rates of relief provided through the ARP
reflect failing medical and grievance systems.
Director Carlson envisioned the ARP serving as an
additional mechanism for resolving issues in prison
quickly and efficiently, but instead, it has become a

III. Too Often, Claims Fail In The ARP Due To
Its Byzantine Rules, Inaction By Prison
Officials, And Blatant Misconduct.
As amici know from experience, in countless cases
claims fail in the ARP not because they lack merit, but
because of the system itself. The types of traps that
can foil a meritorious claim submitted through the
ARP are myriad, including the byzantine rules that
incarcerated people must follow, inaction and delays
by prison officials, and blatant misconduct. See Aala
Abdullahi & Christie Thompson, Grievances in
Federal Prison Rarely Succeed. Here’s How Prisoners
Would Change That , T HE MARSHALL PROJECT (June
14, 2026) (finding that “obtaining relief” through the
ARP’s “complex maze of paperwork” “is nearly
impossible”);15 Christie Thompson & Joseph Shapiro,

(June 13, 2026) (“An unknown number of cases,
especially those involving physical and sexual

of abuse can silence those trying to seek help.”). 16

Byzantine Rules. One of the most common
roadblocks in the ARP is the rules themselves: Prison
officials require rigid adherence to technical rules and
instructions, and reject grievances for any errors,
however minor or trivial. This occurs despite the fact
that BOP policy requires flexibility and
responsiveness in addressing ARP grievances,
expressly discouraging the sort of nitpicking that
happens in practice. See Program Statement 1330.18:
Administrative Remedy Program, U.S.  DEPARTMENT
OF JUSTICE, at 8 (Jan. 16, 2014) (“When deciding
whether to reject a submission, Coordinators,
especially at the institution level, should be flexible,
keeping in mind that major purposes of this program
are to solve problems and be responsive to issues
inmates raise.”).17
There are countless examples of rejections based
on minor errors that should not have prevented the
request from being reviewed on the merits, such as
“writing with a pencil instead of a pen, or a woman
reporting sexual abuse who was rejected for
misspelling her abuser’s last name.” Christie
Thompson et al., ‘Rejected’: How Federal Prisons

These examples are just a handful of countless
variations occurring in federal prisons across the
country. Collectively, they help explain the data
showing that the ARP is not a remedial scheme at all.
Rather, it has become a system used by BOP officials
to frustrate attempts by prisoners to resolve real and
significant problems.
Thus, Petitioner’s notion that this Court should
close federal courts to claims of serious constitutional
violations in federal pris ons because of the ARP is
baseless. The ARP is no alternative to Bivens actions,
which are essential for ensuring that adequate
medical care is provided to people in federal prisons.
Without Bivens actions, people incarcerated in federal
prisons would lack meaningful recourse when their
rights are violated. 26 Accordingly, Petitioner’s
